title: Oxidation and Mechanical Behavior of Nb-Ti-(Cr)-(Al) Refractory Multi-principal Element Alloys at 1000 °C
abstract: Abstract The oxidation and mechanical behavior at 1000 °C of five single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) Nb-Ti-(Cr)-(Al) Refractory Multi-Principal Element Alloys (RMPEAs), with low density of ~ 6.5 g cm −3  and intrinsic room-temperature ductility, was systematically investigated. Isothermal oxidation tests conducted in air for up to 100 h revealed a strongly composition-dependent response. The binary NbTi alloy exhibited near-linear oxidation kinetics and an extensive internal reaction zone (IRZ). Conversely, Cr- and Al-containing alloys demonstrated reduced mass gain, narrowed IRZ and altered kinetic regimes, attributed to the formation of chemically complex oxide scales. Although Cr and Al additions reduced both mass gain and IRZ, oxide-scale spallation persisted across all compositions. Compression tests at 1000 °C confirmed that all alloys retained ductile behavior, with Cr-containing compositions exhibiting superior yield strength. Among the evaluated alloys, Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  achieved the most favorable balance between oxidation resistance (mass gain of 14.4 mg cm −2  after 100 h of exposure) and mechanical stability (yield strength 229.0 MPa at 1000 °C). The combined addition of Cr and Al to the equimolar NbTi alloy improves oxidation resistance and mechanical performance, advancing the development of lightweight RMPEAs for high-temperature structural applications.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Refractory High-Entropy Alloys (RHEAs) or Refractory Multi-Principal Element Alloy (RMPEAs), have recently emerged as a new generation of metallic materials designed to retain their mechanical properties at elevated temperatures (Ref  1 ,  2 ,  3 ,  4 ,  5 - 6 ). However, development of RMPEAs capable of forming stable and continuous protective oxide layers remains a challenge. To prevent direct gas-metal contact, it is essential to facilitate the formation of protective surface layers, such as Al 2 O 3 , Cr 2 O 3  or SiO 2  (Ref  7 ,  8 ,  9 - 10 ). The formation of these protective scales can be achieved either by tailoring the bulk alloy composition to promote selective oxidation or by applying coating technologies designed to react in high-temperature oxidizing environments (Ref  11 ,  12 ,  13 ,  14 - 15 ).

Typically, RMPEAs form complex oxides with limited protective capabilities, often exhibiting linear or quasi-parabolic oxidation kinetics (Ref  16 ,  17 - 18 ). Nevertheless, specific compounds such as CrNbO 4  and AlNbO 4 , have shown particular promise and are recognized for their ability to enhance high-temperature oxidation resistance (Ref  18 ,  19 ). The presence of these oxides has been reported in several metallic systems, including Nb-Cr and Nb-Al, where their formation is associated with decelerated oxidation kinetics (Ref  20 ,  21 ,  22 ,  23 ,  24 - 25 ). Butler et al. (Ref  18 ) emphasized this effect by reporting quasi-parabolic oxidation kinetics in a Nb-Ti-Zr-Cr alloy, attributed to the formation of CrNbO 4  at 1000 °C. Similarly, Zhu et al. (Ref  19 ) identified the remarkable stability of AlNbO 4  in the Ti-Nb-V-Al alloys at 800 °C.

Beyond the challenges associated with achieving satisfactory oxidation resistance, the design of RMPEAs also presents limitations related to their intrinsically high density and restricted room temperature ductility (Ref  8 ,  26 ,  27 ,  28 - 29 ). For instance, in systems such as Ta-Mo-Cr-Ti-Al, studied by Gorr et al. (Ref  30 ), Chen et al. (Ref  31 ) and others (Ref  32 ,  33 - 34 ), satisfactory oxidation behavior has been attributed to the formation of complex (Cr,Ta)O 2 -type oxides. These oxides display rutile-like structures and exhibits higher thermodynamic stability than the well-known Cr 2 O 3  (Ref  35 ). Consequently, these layers act as effective diffusion barriers, limiting outward cation transport and possess growth rates intermediate to those characteristics of Cr 2 O 3  and Al 2 O 3  scales (Ref  36 ).

In this alloy system, each element contributes distinctly to oxide-scale development. Cr and Ta promote the formation of mixed Cr-Ta oxides, Al enhances the initial nucleation of Cr 2 O 3 , and the Ti contributes to stabilizing the rutile-type structure (Ref  22 ,  35 ,  37 ). However, such alloys exhibit a relatively high density (~ 8.6 g cm −3 ) and limited ductility, characteristics attributed to the simultaneous presence of ordered B2 and Laves phases (Ref  33 ,  36 ). Thus, the incorporating lower-density elements is a strategic approach for designing lighter RMPEAs capable of maintaining toughness and high-temperature performance.

In this context, Nb-Ti-based systems have attracted considerable interest for the development of low-density RMPEAs. These systems enable the design of alloys with densities of ~ 6.5 g cm −3  and combining reduced weight with a high melting point, and satisfactory formability even at room temperature. In Nb-containing solid-solutions alloys, the addition of Ti is well known to enhance ductility and fracture toughness (Ref  38 ,  39 ). Aluminum also plays a critical role, as it not only reduces density but also contributes to improved oxidation resistance (Ref  40 ,  41 ). However, excessive Al contents may cause significant lattice distortion and promote the formation of intermetallic compounds, resulting in a loss of ductility (Ref  42 ).

Furthermore, while Al stabilizes the body-centered cubic (BCC) phase and may induce partial B2 ordering (Ref  43 ,  44 ), Cr is widely used to improve creep resistance and to promote the formation of protective oxide layers (Ref  45 ). However, Cr also tends to nucleate brittle phase in multicomponent BCC alloys. For example, Senkov et al. (Ref  46 ) reported intergranular fracture and limited plastic deformation in CrNbTiZr and CrNbTiVZr alloys, attributing these phenomena to the presence of Laves phase.

Titanium aluminide (TiAl)-based alloys, such as Ti-48Al-2Cr-2Nb, are notable for their low density and high specific strength, and they are widely applied in aerospace and automotive components at intermediate temperatures up to ~ 700 °C. Nevertheless, their intrinsic room-temperature brittleness and accelerated oxidation at higher temperatures remain major obstacles to broader implementation (Ref  47 ,  48 ). In contrast, Ni-based superalloys remain the benchmark for applications up to 1100 °C, although they exhibit considerably high density (> 8 g cm −3 ) (Ref  49 ,  50 ). Consequently, a clear technological gap persists between TiAl-based alloys and Ni-based superalloys. This defines a temperature and performance window for which materials that simultaneously offering low density, mechanical strength, and satisfactory oxidation resistance are still lacking.

Against this background, Nb-Ti-based RMPEAs alloys have emerged as a promising alternative, combining low density, high melting point, and good formability. However, their oxidation resistance remains insufficient for demanding high-temperature environments (Ref  51 ,  52 - 53 ). Despite the growing interest in these systems, the literature still lacks systematic investigations addressing the individual and combined effects of Cr and Al additions to the Nb-Ti system, particularly regarding oxidation behavior.

In a previous study, five RMPEAs within the Nb-Ti-(Cr)-(Al) system were designed through thermodynamic calculations and 2 2  factorial design with central point. The combined Cr and Al content was restricted to 25 at.% to avoid the formation of intermetallic phases such as B2 and Laves. These alloys were characterized in terms of microstructure and mechanical performance, revealing a disordered BCC solid solution with dendritic morphology. Compositional segregation was governed by melting-point differences, leading Ti, Cr, and Al to partition preferentially into interdendritic regions. Furthermore, the alloys also exhibited a low density (~ 6.5 g cm −3 ) combined with high mechanical strength and ductile behavior at room temperature (Ref  54 ). However, the oxidation behavior and mechanical performance at 1000 °C of these alloys have not yet been investigated.

Therefore, building upon previous findings (Ref  54 ), the present study aims to evaluate the oxidation behavior of NbTi, Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2 , Nb 7 Ti 7 Al 2 , Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1  and Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  RMPEAs in ambient air at 1000 °C for exposure times of up to 100 h. Additionally, this study assesses their mechanical performance under compression at 1000 °C, in comparison with previously reported room-temperature results, in order to evaluate the potential of these alloys for high-temperature structural applications.

sections.heading: Materials and Methods
paragraphs: The alloys NbTi, Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2 , Nb 7 Ti 7 Al 2 , Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1  e Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1 , designated as  A1 ,  A2 ,  A3 ,  A4 , and  A5 , respectively, were synthesized from high-purity elements (99.95 wt.%) in a water-cooled copper crucible arc-melting furnace under a high-purity argon atmosphere, employing titanium as a getter. Each ingot was re-melted at least five times, with inversion between melting cycles, to enhance chemical homogeneity, resulting in a single-phase BCC solid solution exhibiting dendritic morphology (Ref  54 ). The alloy designations, nominal and experimental compositions, and density values are summarized in Table  1 . Chemical compositions were determined by energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV, while experimental density measurements were performed according to Archimedes’ principle in water at room temperature. Table 1 Alloy designation, chemical composition based on energy-dispersive x-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis and measured densities of the developed RMPEAs Alloy Designation Composition, at.% Density, g cm −3 Nb Ti Cr Al Nb 7 Ti 7 A1 Nom. 50.00 50.00 … … 6.86 ± 0.23 Exp. 50.16 49.84 … … Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2 A2 Nom. 43.75 43.75 12.50 … 6.62 ± 0.07 Exp. 42.80 44.53 12.63 … Nb 7 Ti 7 Al 2 A3 Nom. 43.75 43.75 … 12.50 6.12 ± 0.09 Exp. 44.10 43.77 … 12.16 Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1 A4 Nom. 43.75 43.75 6.25 6.25 6.40 ± 0.08 Exp. 43.37 44.00 6.47 6.10 Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1 A5 Nom. 37.50 37.50 12.50 12.50 6.35 ± 0.12 Exp. 37.27 37.70 12.70 12.37

For oxidation testing, specimens of approximately (5 × 5 × 5) mm 3  were sectioned from the ingots using a Struers Accutom precision cutter. All specimens were prepared using the same surface preparation procedure. The specimen surfaces were ground to #1000 grit finish using SiC paper, followed by ultrasonic cleaning in isopropyl alcohol for 15 min. Isothermal oxidation tests in ambient air were conducted in a tubular furnace at 1000 °C, with exposure times of 1, 20, 60, and 100 h. For each alloy and exposure time, three independent specimens were simultaneously evaluated under the same conditions, and each sample was exposed only once. The specimens were placed in alumina crucibles, inserted directly into the hot zone of the preheated furnace, and subsequently subjected to natural cooling in air. Spalled oxides retained in the alumina crucibles were carefully collected and included in the mass gain measurements. Mass change measurements were performed using a semi-micro balance with a resolution of 0.01 mg.

Post-oxidation structural characterization was carried out via x-ray diffraction (XRD) on powders extracted from the oxidized surface, using a PANalytical Empyrean diffractometer in Bragg-Brentano geometry ( θ -2 θ ) with a step size of 0.04° and a scan rate of 2 s/step, employing Cu K α 1  radiation ( λ  = 0.15406 nm). Phase identification and peak indexing were executed using High Score Plus software. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) of both surface and cross-sectional regions was conducted using an Oxford SwiftED3000 EDS detector operating at 20 kV.

For cross-sectional characterization, the oxidized specimens were mounted in polyester resin, ground with SiC paper, polished with a colloidal silica suspension, and ultrasonically cleaned in isopropyl alcohol for 15 min. The thickness of the internal reaction zone (IRZ) was quantified from backscattered electron (BSE) images using ImageJ software, with average values and standard deviations calculated from 25 distinct measurements taken across three different regions for each sample.

Compression tests were performed at room temperature (25 °C) and at 1000 °C. Cylindrical specimens were prepared by wire electrical discharge machining (WEDM) to dimensions of 5.0 mm in height and 3.3 mm in diameter, strictly maintaining a height-to-diameter (h/d) ratio of 1.5 in accordance with the DIN 50106 standard (Ref  55 ). The tests were conducted on a Zwick/Roell Z050 universal testing machine equipped with SiC plates and high-precision extensometers, under a constant strain rate of 1 mm.min −1 . The tests were manually interrupted before reaching a maximum load of 10 kN or upon exceeding an engineering strain of 25%. All testing conditions were evaluated in triplicate to ensure reproducibility and statistical reliability.

sections.heading: Isothermal Oxidation Kinetics
paragraphs: Figure  1 (a) illustrates the specific mass-gain curves of the five developed RMPEAs subjected to isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C in ambient air. The corresponding linearized data are presented in Fig.  1 (b), while Fig.  1 (c) displays the surface appearance of the specimens after 100 h of exposure. Fig. 1 Experimental mass gain per area of the developed RMPEAs during isothermal oxidation in ambient air at 1000 °C for up to 100 h: (a) Linear plot; (b) Natural logarithmic plot; (c) Macro-morphology after 1, 20, 60 and 100 h of exposure

The time exponent,  n , defines the kinetic regime: values approaching  n  ≈ 1 indicate linear behavior, which is typically associated with oxide growth lacking effective diffusion barriers at either the gas-oxide or metal-oxide interfaces. This regime generally results in poorly adherent, defect-rich scales that allow continuous gas transport (Ref  56 ,  57 ). Conversely,  n  ≈ 0.5 corresponds to parabolic kinetics, characteristic of diffusion-controlled growth and the formation of dense, adherent, and protective oxide layers with a low defect density. Intermediate values between 1 and 0.5 reflect mixed kinetic regimes, whereas  n  < 0.5 denotes sub-parabolic behavior, frequently associated with partial volatilization of the oxides or the development of porous scales (Ref  56 ,  57 ).

The calculated kinetic parameters,  k  and  n , are summarized in Table  2 . A distinct reduction in the  n  values is observed upon the addition of Cr and Al, indicating that these elements fundamentally modify the oxidation mechanism at 1000 °C. This kinetic shift aligns with the specific mass-gain responses illustrated in Fig.  1 (a) and (b). Table 2 Experimental mass gain and calculated kinetics parameters, including the coefficient of determination ( R 2 ), after 100 h of oxidation at 1000 °C in ambient air of the developed RMPEAs Alloy Δ W/A  100 h, mg cm −2 n k,  mg cm −2  h − n R 2 A1 249.52 ± 16.30 0.83 5.41 0.99 A2 100.64 ± 0.50 0.74 2.50 0.96 A3 88.00 ± 4.30 0.67 3.45 0.96 A4 67.45 ± 1.30 0.72 2.33 0.98 A5 14.40 ± 0.20 0.45 1.54 0.96

Table  2  reveals a clear composition-dependent transition in oxidation kinetics. At 1000 °C, the binary  A1  alloy exhibited a time exponent of 0.83, denoting near-linear behavior ( n  ≈ 1). In contrast, the simultaneous addition of Cr and Al in the  A5  alloy reduced the time exponent to 0.45, indicating a shift toward a regime closer to parabolic behavior ( n  ≈ 0.5). The intermediate alloys ( A2-A4 ) exhibited  n  values between these limits, reflecting mixed kinetic regimes governed by both interfacial reactions and diffusion. These findings corroborate a progressive transition in the oxidation mechanism driven by the concentration of Cr and Al.

Despite this transition toward parabolic tendencies upon the incorporation of Cr and Al, the resulting oxide scales remained poorly adherent and defect-rich across all compositions, including alloy  A5 . This structural instability promoted macroscopic oxide spallation, as visibly confirmed in Fig.  1 (c). The non-protective properties of Nb-rich RMPEAs are likely attributable the transient formation and multiple polymorphic transformations of Nb 2 O 5  oxide, which induce volumetric expansion and subsequent crack formation and chipping (Ref  35 ). Although the spalled oxides were collected and included in the mass gain measurements, assessing of oxidation resistance solely based on specific mass-gain data remains inherently unreliable, as it is strongly affected by oxide loss.

To circumvent this limitation, quantitative analysis of the internal reaction zone (IRZ) thickness is essential. The IRZ depth is independent of scale spallation and provides a more reliable metric for evaluating the true barrier capability of oxide layer. The penetration of oxygen and nitrogen into the substrate, subsequently confirmed by EDS analysis, drives the formation of this sub-scale reaction zone (Ref  58 ). The extent of the IRZ is inversely proportional to the protectiveness of the external scale; highly protective oxides yield proportionally narrower IRZ thickness (Ref  59 ,  60 ). Figure  2  presents cross-sectional micrographs of the IRZ after 20 h of exposure. This specific timeframe was selected to bypass the transient oxidation stages prevalent at 1 h, while avoiding the severe scale degradation observed at 60 and 100 h, thus ensuring a highly representative evaluation of IRZ. Fig. 2 IRZ characterization of the developed RMPEAs after isothermal oxidation at 1000 °C for 20 h in ambient air: (a) Measured depth of the IRZ; (b) Cross-sectional BSE-SEM images highlighting the external oxide layer and the extent of the IRZ for each respective composition

As illustrated in Fig.  2 , the binary  A1  alloy developed a permeable, non-protective oxide layer that facilitated extensive oxygen diffusion. This resulted in a deeper IRZ that compromised the entire specimen thickness, thereby confirming the absence of an effective barrier mechanism (Ref  51 ). In contrast, the Cr and/or Al-containing alloys exhibited significantly restricted IRZ depth, indicating that these additions substantially enhance the oxidation resistance of the binary NbTi base system, corroborating the kinetics data in Table  2 .

After 20 h of exposure at 1000 °C, the measured IRZ depths were 71.6 ( A2 ), 155.8 ( A3 ), 90.9 ( A4 ), and 49.9 µm ( A5 ). These values establish a direct correlation between alloy chemistry and environmental ingress kinetics. Alloy  A5 , possessing the highest combined concentration of Cr and Al, exhibited the shallowest IRZ, followed progressively by  A2 ,  A4 , and  A3 . This hierarchy underscores the dominant role of Cr in dictating oxidation resistance. Increased Cr availability promotes the preferential nucleation and growth of dense Cr-rich oxides (e.g., Cr 2 O 3 ). This oxide layer acts as a diffusion barrier, effectively separating the metal from the oxidizing environment, which suppresses oxygen ingress and limits subsequent IRZ development (Ref  51 ,  61 ,  62 ).

This mechanism aligns with thermodynamic and kinetic frameworks reported by Dahshan et al. (Ref  63 ), who evaluated the oxidation behavior of Co + Cr 23 C 6  alloy in air between 900 to 1100 °C. Their findings demonstrate that the formation of a protective Cr 2 O 3  scale is predominantly governed by chromium availability within the alloy, rather than its activity, a conclusion derived from equilibrium thermodynamics and Fick’s first law. The availability of chromium governs the outward diffusion of Cr toward the surface and the subsequent development of a continuous and dense oxide layer. This Cr 2 O 3  scale effectively restricts inward oxygen transport, decelerating the overall reaction rate and commonly promoting parabolic kinetics (Ref  64 ,  65 ).

Furthermore, comparing the microstructural response of  A3  and  A2  (Fig.  2 ), reveals that substituting Cr with an equivalent atomic fraction of Al significantly deepens the IRZ. This indicates that Al is less effective than Cr in improving oxidation resistance in this specific base system. Although Al 2 O 3  is recognized as a highly protective oxide, characterized by parabolic kinetics and efficient oxygen diffusion barrier properties (Ref  51 ,  62 ,  66 ), the 12.5 at.% Al addition in  A3  was insufficient to promote the formation of a continuous and stable Al 2 O 3  scale. This critical concentration limitation is consistent with literature indicating that certain RMPEAs fail to establish continuous Al 2 O 3  scales even at Al concentration reaching 20 at.% (Ref  62 ). Conversely, the 71.6 µm IRZ depth observed in the Cr-containing  A2  alloy exhibits strong parity with the 84.0 µm depth reported by Welch et al. (Ref  60 ) for an equiatomic TaTiCr alloy oxidized at 1000 °C for 24 h, where internal degradation similarly manifested as coarse lenticular precipitates distributed within the BCC matrix.

The morphological characteristics of the IRZ in the present study agree well with previous investigations of similar systems. Butler et al. (Ref  67 ) reported that the oxidation of a CrNbTi alloy at 1200 °C for 24 h generated an IRZ comprising complex sub-scale products, including TiO 2 , Cr 2 O 3 , Nb 2 N, Cr 3 Nb 3 N, and deep-penetrating TiN precipitates interspersed with Laves phase and remnant BCC matrix. Similarly, Tang et al. (Ref  59 ) observed that internal nitridation during the oxidation of Ti-Mo-Ta-Cr-Al RMPEAs (900-1100 °C) induced the precipitation of extensive needle-shaped TiN particles beneath the oxide layer, which was accompanied by scale spallation at the metal-oxide interface. As illustrated in Fig.  2 (b), the alloys investigated herein developed a comparable IRZ morphology, characterized by a continuous sub-surface layer of precipitates distributed within the matrix, as will be discussed in subsequent sections.

sections.heading: Surface Analysis
paragraphs: Figure  3  presents the x-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns used to identify the oxide layer composition of the five developed RMPEAs after 100 h of exposure in ambient air at 1000 °C. Figure  3 (a) compares the full diffraction patterns of the alloys, whereas Fig.  3 (b) and (c) highlight the diffraction regions corresponding to rutile-type and (Ti, Nb)-mixed oxides, respectively. Fig. 3 XRD patterns of the developed RMPEAs after oxidation at 1000 °C in ambient air for 100 h: (a) All five alloys; (b, c) Detailed view of the XRD patterns

Comparison of the diffraction patterns in Fig.  3 (a) indicates that the binary NbTi alloy ( A1 ) forms two main crystalline oxides, TiNb 2 O 7  (space group C2/m) and rutile (TiO 2  prototype, space group P4 2 /mnm). No traces of the binary Nb 2 O 5  oxide were detected in the XRD patterns. Similar results have been reported for Ti-Nb-based alloys (Ref  9 ,  10 ,  18 ,  52 ,  53 ), where the dominant oxidation products were TiO 2 , TiNb 2 O 7  or higher-order complex oxides. Based on Ellingham diagrams, the preferential formation of TiO 2  during the initial stages of oxidation is anticipated due to its superior thermodynamic stability compared to Nb 2 O 5  (Ref  21 ,  53 ). Consequently, the subsequent reaction between TiO 2  and Nb 2 O 5  to form the more stable TiNb 2 O 7  complex oxide (Ref  19 ) likely suppresses the retention of isolated Nb 2 O 5  within the oxide scale.

Upon the addition of 12.5 at.% Cr ( A2 ), additional peaks corresponding to Cr 2 O 3  (space group R-3c) emerged, while the diffraction signals for TiNb 2 O 7  and rutile persisted. Similarly, in the alloy containing 12.5 at.% Al ( A3 ), low-intensity peaks attributed to AlNbO 4  (space group C2/m) were detected, coexisting with the diffraction peaks of TiNb 2 O 7  and rutile. The absence of diffraction peaks corresponding to corundum-type Al 2 O 3  (space group R-3c), suggests that this Al content is insufficient to promote the formation of a continuous and stable Al 2 O 3  scale.

For the quaternary alloys containing both Cr and Al,  A4  (12.5 at.% combined) and  A5  (25.0 at.% combined), the oxide phases formed were similar to those observed in  A2 , indicating that Cr 2 O 3  remains stable even at relatively low Cr concentrations. In these alloys, shifts in the 2 θ  positions of the Cr 2 O 3  peaks were observed, suggesting the formation of a (Cr, Al) 2 O 3  solid solution. Such solid solutions are frequently reported during the oxidation of multi-component alloys containing both Al and Cr (Ref  68 ,  69 ,  70 - 71 ). Furthermore, consistent with the observations for the  A1  alloy, no evidence of Nb 2 O 5  was detected in the Cr- and Al-containing alloys ( A2  -  A5 ). It is thought that the formation of thermodynamically more stable complex oxides, such as AlNbO 4  and CrNbO 4 , tends to neutralize the presence of Nb 2 O 5  via its reaction with Al 2 O 3  and Cr 2 O 3 , respectively (Ref  19 ,  20 ,  67 ). The formation of these complex oxides has been associated with improved oxidation resistance in refractory alloys (Ref  19 ,  20 ), which is consistent with the reduced mass gains observed for the Cr- and Al-containing alloys in Fig.  1 (a).

A closer analysis of Fig.  3  reveals systematic shifts in the rutile-type diffraction peaks, for example at approximately 2 θ  ≈ 27.4° (110) and 36.1° (101), as highlighted in the detailed view of XRD in Fig.  3 (b). These shifts in the 2 θ  angle, along with peak splitting observed as a function of the alloy compositions, indicate variations in the lattice parameters of the post-oxidation rutile-type oxides. These variations are likely associated with the formation of complex rutile solid solutions incorporating different proportions of Nb, Ti, Cr, and Al derived from the substrate (Ref  59 ).

Several ternary or more complex oxides with rutile structure relevant to this system have been reported (Ref  20 ,  35 ,  67 ,  72 ), including NbTiO 4 , CrNbO 4 , (Nb,Cr)O 2 , and (Nb,Ti,Al)O 2 , all of which are analogous to TiO 2 . These compounds exhibit distinct lattice parameters: NbTiO 4  (PDF No 01-081-0911) with  a  = 4.7430 and  c  = 2.9944 Å; CrNbO 4  (PDF No 01-081-0909),  a  = 4.6484 and  c  = 3.0113 Å; (Nb,Cr)O 2  (PDF No 01-074-6530),  a  = 4.6450 and  c  = 2.0140 Å; and (Nb,Cr,Al)O 2  (PDF No 01-079-1187),  a  = 4.5849 and  c  = 2.9599 Å. These values differ from the lattice parameters of pure rutile TiO 2  ( a  = 4.5928,  c  = 2.9582 Å), directly accounting for the noticeable variations in the 2 θ  positions of the observed diffraction peaks.

A similar effect is observed in the Fig.  3 (c) for the TiNb 2 O 7  phase in the Cr-containing alloys ( A2 ,  A4  and  A5 ). Previous studies have reported that the incorporation of Cr 3+  can reduce the characteristic peak splitting associated with the monoclinic C2/m structure of TiNb 2 O 7 , as its ionic radius (0.62 Å) closely matches that of Ti 4+  (0.61 Å). This similarity facilitates structurally compatible substitution, thereby mitigating local lattice distortion (Ref  73 ,  74 - 75 ). The present results further suggest that Cr additions may promote partial structural rearrangement toward the orthorhombic Ti 2 Nb 10 O 29  phase (Amma). In contrast, the significantly smaller ionic radius of Al 3+  (0.53 Å) introduces a greater lattice mismatch, thereby preserving or even intensifying the local monoclinic distortion (Ref  74 ,  76 ). Consequently, while a partial transition to Ti 2 Nb 10 O 29  cannot be entirely ruled out, the dominant effect remains the Al-induced lattice distortion, which sustains the observed peak splitting.

Building upon the phase constitution identified by XRD (Fig.  3 ), surface micrographs of the oxide layers formed on the five RMPEAs after 20 h of oxidation in ambient air at 1000 °C are presented in Fig.  4 . These scanning electron microscopy (SEM) images reveal morphological differences among the alloys. Furthermore, local chemical variations determined by EDS (Table  3 ) corroborate the oxide phases identified by XRD. Fig. 4 Surface SEM images of the developed RMPEAs after oxidation at 1000 °C in ambient air for 20 h: (a) NbTi ( A1 ); (b) Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2  ( A2 ); (c) Nb 7 Ti 7 Al 2  ( A3 ); (d) Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1  ( A4 ); (e) Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  ( A5 ) Table 3 Semi-quantitative microanalyses obtained via EDS at different points on the surface of developed RMPEAs following 20 h of oxidation at 1000 °C in ambient air Alloy EDS Elements, at.% Nb Ti Cr Al O A1 1 10.9 15.3 … … 73.7 A2 1 7.6 18.6 7.8 … 66.0 2 0.8 28.3 1.8 … 69.1 A3 1 17.9 16.2 4.6 61.3 A4 1 5.8 20.9 1.5 3.9 67.8 2 19.1 16.1 1.8 3.0 60.0 A5 1 4.8 12.0 5.1 7.6 70.5 2 8.4 12.0 5.7 6.4 67.4

As shown in Fig.  4 (a), the surface of alloy  A1  is characterized by a single, fragmented, and highly porous layer composed predominantly of Ti-Nb-oxides (EDS: Ti ≈ 15, Nb ≈ 11, O ≈ 74 at.%). This composition agrees with the TiNb 2 O 7  phase identified by XRD. The irregular morphology suggests a high susceptibility to oxygen ingress (Ref  57 ), directly reflecting the intensive IRZ depth previously observed in Fig.  2 .

In contrast, alloy  A3  shows a relatively homogeneous surface featuring fine particles, dispersed porosity, and a moderate Al content (≈ 5 at.%). Compared to  A1 , this surface exhibits fewer defects, indicative of a marginally improved oxide scale, which correlates with the reduced IRZ depth measured in Fig.  2 .

Figure  4 (b), (d) and (e), highlight that the Cr-containing alloys ( A2 ,  A4 , and  A5 ) exhibit two distinct surface regions under BSE-SEM imaging. In alloy  A2 , the addition of 12.5 at.% Cr promoted the formation of coarse, faceted, and relatively compact TiO 2  (rutile), which coexist with finer, porous regions enriched in Nb and Cr. This structural evolution aligns with the results of Guo et al. (Ref  77 ), who reported pronounced oxide grain growth proportional to increasing Cr content in MoNbVTa 0.5 Cr x  alloys.

Although Cr additions contribute to the development of denser, more stable layers, they simultaneously induce morphological heterogeneities. These localized variations can generate internal stresses and scale spallation, as evident in the Fig.  1 (c). Tang et al. (Ref  36 ) reported similar stress-induced spallation in the Ti-Mo-Ta-Cr-Al system at oxidized in air at 1000 °C. Moreover, residual pores and cracks acts as preferential fast-diffusion pathways for oxygen, intensifying oxidation, a phenomenon also discussed by Guo et al. (Ref  77 ).

Figure  4 (d) demonstrates localized surface segregation in alloy  A4 , characterized by coalesced Ti-rich oxides (dark regions in BSE-SEM) and fine Nb-rich oxides (bright regions in BSE-SEM), exhibiting a morphology analogous to that of  A2 . These topographic disparities correlate with the formation of complex rutile-type oxides and mixed Ti-Nb oxides, as confirmed via XRD. Clear evidence of oxide spallation is also visible, which compromises the continuity of the protective barrier.

Finally, Fig.  4 (e) reveals that the surface of alloy  A5  features dense, undulated (hill-like) regions alternating with porous domains, notably lacking significant compositional variance between these adjacent zones. This morphology is analogous to that reported by Lu et al. (Ref  20 ) regarding Al additions in the AlMo 0.5 NbTa 0.5 TiZr system, where inherent microsegregation between dendritic and interdendritic regions led to the formation of different complex oxides, ultimately inducing localized scale detachment and cracking.

sections.heading: Cross-Section Analysis
paragraphs: Representative cross-sectional BSE-SEM micrographs and corresponding EDS maps of the five developed RMPEAs after 20 h of oxidation in ambient air at 1000 °C are shown in Fig.  5 . These images reveal the development of complex oxide scales distinguished by specific morphological and compositional features. The EDS line scans (Fig.  6 ) validate the presence of compositional gradients across the oxide layers and IRZ. Notably, alloys containing 12.5 at.% Cr exhibited a highly complex, multilayered scale architecture, suggesting a transition in the governing oxidation mechanism at this specific chromium concentration. The EDS points identified in Fig.  5  are summarized in Table  4 . Fig. 5 Representative cross-sectional BSE-SEM images and corresponding EDS maps of the developed RMPEAs after 20 h of oxidation at 1000 °C: (a) NbTi ( A1 ); (b) Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2  ( A2 ); (c) Nb 7 Ti 7 Al 2  ( A3 ); (d) Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1  ( A4 ); (e) Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  ( A5 ) Fig. 6 EDS Line scans of the developed RMPEAs after 20 h of oxidation at 1000 °C: (a) NbTi ( A1 ); (b) Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2  ( A2 ); (c) Nb 7 Ti 7 Al 2  ( A3 ); (d) Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1  ( A4 ); (e) Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  ( A5 ) Table 4 EDS point analyses of oxide scale regions in the developed RMPEAs after 20 h oxidation at 1000 °C (Fig.  5 ) Alloy Spot Elements, at.% Nb Ti Cr Al O N A1 1 14.9 13.4 … … 71.7 0.0 2 9.9 23.8 … … 66.1 0.2 A2 1 15.0 16.2 7.2 … 61.6 0.0 2 5.6 28.3 9.7 … 56.3 0.0 3 9.1 16.0 15.7 … 59.3 0.0 A3 1 19.0 14.4 … 3.7 63.0 0.0 2 16.7 17.8 … 4.3 61.2 0.0 A4 1 19.8 13.7 2.1 2.0 62.4 0.0 2 13.5 18.1 3.3 2.8 62.3 0.0 3 15.5 30.7 6.2 4.0 43.6 0.0 A5 1 24.3 15.0 5.1 2.6 53.0 0.0 2 12.1 17.7 7.9 1.2 61.0 0.0 3 11.7 29.9 14.5 2.4 41.6 0.0

Across all alloys, oxidation culminated in the formation of a multilayered external oxide scale followed by a nitrogen-enriched subsurface region located immediately beneath the metal-oxide interface. This nitrogen-rich layer is particularly evident in the EDS line scans (Fig.  6 ), where a pronounced increase in nitrogen content coincides with the onset of the IRZ. This phenomenon demonstrates that inward nitrogen diffusion proceeds concurrently with oxygen permeation, a synergistic degradation mechanism similarly documented by Tang et al. (Ref  59 ).

In the binary NbTi alloy ( A1 ), the oxide scale involved into a porous, stratified layer characterized by profound cracking, widespread voids formation (“holes”), and local spallation (Fig.  5 a). These defects establish unhindered, fast-diffusion for oxygen anions (O 2 ⁻), facilitating rapid access to the oxide-substrate interface. As confirmed by EDS (Table  4 ) and XRD analysis, the scale is predominantly composed of TiNb 2 O 7  and TiO 2 . The TiNb 2 O 7  phase possesses a high Pilling-Bedworth ratio (PBR ≈ 2.69), which likely contributes to the generation of compressive growth stresses within the oxide scale, especially when compared against the TiO 2  phase (PBR ≈ 1.73) (Ref  19 ). This mismatch fundamentally explains the cracking and interfacial detachment observed in  A1 . Micro-cracking of the oxide scale normally arises from stress accumulation within the scale (Ref  59 ,  67 ), which in this case is dictated by simultaneous grown of dissimilar-PBR oxides and progressive scale thickening. Consistent with the literature, the dominance of TiNb 2 O 7  is associated with the non-protective, near-linear oxidation kinetics characteristic of Nb-Ti-based systems (Ref  18 ,  51 ,  53 ).

For the Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2  alloy ( A2 ), the addition of Cr clearly promotes segregation within the oxide scale, yielding a coarser, heavily portioned multi-oxide morphology relative to  A1 , as illustrated in Fig.  5 (b). The scale architecture comprises three primary regions: an outermost dual-layer of TiO 2  and Cr 2 O 3 , trailed by an intermediate zone of discontinuous, alternating TiNb 2 O 7  and TiO 2  strata. This specific microstructural configuration is confirmed by the EDS elemental mapping (Fig.  5 b) and EDS line scanning (Fig.  6 b), with corresponding chemical compositions provided in Table  4 .

Tang et al. (Ref  59 ), reported a comparable layered oxide architecture after oxidizing Ti-Mo-Ta-Cr-Al RMPEAs at 1000 °C for 24 h. Their structure consisted of an external TiO 2  surface layer situated above a (Cr, Al) 2 O 3  solid solution, terminating in refractory-rich sublayers, a configuration mirroring the present findings, though the innermost sublayer herein is Nb-enriched. Crucially, the profile in Fig.  5 (b) indicates that the Cr 2 O 3 -rich domain remains discontinuous. In Cr-based alloys, Cr 2 O 3  typically forms a compact, continuous, and protective scale adhering to parabolic growth kinetics (Ref  23 ,  24 ,  78 ). As demonstrated by Guo et al. (Ref  77 ), incrementally raising the Cr content in MoNbVTa 0.5 Cr x  alloys markedly enhances oxidation resistance, indicating that higher baseline Cr concentrations are required to stabilize a continuous Cr 2 O 3  layer in Nb-Ti-based systems.

In the Al-containing Nb 7 Ti 7 Al 2  alloy ( A3 ), the oxide scale morphology closely resembles that of  A1  (Fig.  5 c). The degradation zone consists of discontinuous, alternating layers of TiNb 2 O 7  and TiO 2 , with no trace of a continuous Al 2 O 3 -rich layer, as confirmed by the attenuated Al signal in both the EDS maps and line scans (Fig.  5 c and  6 c). Furthermore, the nitrogen line scan (Fig.  6 c) again reveals a distinct N-enriched band stationed immediately beneath the oxide scale, directly correlating with extensive subsurface precipitation of TiN within the IRZ. These observations confirm that the 12.5 at.% Al content in  A3  is insufficient to drive selective oxidation and stabilization of a protective alumina scale under these specific thermal parameters.

For the Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1  alloy ( A4 ), which incorporates combined additions of Cr and Al, the overall oxide-scale morphology remains dominated by discontinuous TiNb 2 O 7 /TiO 2  layers (Fig.  5 d). Alongside localized enrichment within the scale, the outermost region exhibits enrichment in Ti, Cr, and Nb, suggesting the formation of a chemically complex oxide, presumed to hold a rutile-type structure. However, the well-defined segregation layers similar to those observed in  A2  are absent. The EDS line scan (Fig.  6 d) again tracks an acute nitrogen peak positioned directly below the oxide layer, confirming that nitrogen ingress and IRZ development persist despite the dual incorporation of these elements at the specific concentration.

The Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 1 Al 1  alloy ( A5 ) exhibits the most complex oxide morphology, characterized by a discontinuous agglomeration of multiple oxide layers. Because  A5  shares an equivalent Cr content with  A2 , its scale architecture similarly displays pronounced segregation sublayers. Specifically, this translates to an external dual-layer scale, a mid-region composed of alternating TiNb 2 O 7  and TiO 2 , and an interior defined by discrete Cr-rich and Ti-rich strata. These segregated regions are highlighted in Fig.  5 (e). The robust validity of this structural model is supported by the EDS line scan in Fig.  6 (e) and the chemical compositions recorded in Table  4 .

Beyond the Ti-, Cr-, and Nb-enriched outer layer, a feature shared with  A4  and highly indicative of complex rutile-type oxides, the central portion of the scale exhibits the formation of a (Cr, Al) 2 O 3  solid solution. This synergistic mechanism aligns with the findings reported by Tang et al. (Ref  59 ), who proved that the mutual dissolution of Cr 2 O 3  and Al 2 O 3  fundamentally promotes the stabilization of dense, mixed-oxide scales in refractory systems. Beneath this region, discontinuous layers of TiNb 2 O 7  and TiO 2  are observed.

The RMPEAs oxidized at 1000 °C yielded post-oxidation microstructures dominated by discontinuous, repetitively stratified scales composed primarily of TiO 2  and TiNb 2 O 7  (in alloys  A1 ,  A3 , and  A4 ). This morphology reflects inherent kinetic limitations and aligns with the near-linear growth regimes typical of base Nb-Ti systems, wherein these phases are identified as non-protective products, as reported by Senkov et al. (Ref  79 ). In contrast, Cr-containing alloys  A2  and  A5  developed pronounced segregation sublayers defined by a TiO 2  and Cr 2 O 3  dual-layer architecture. This structure indicates enhanced outward cation diffusion, typically associated with superior oxidation resistance in refractory alloys. Although these specific microstructural developments share trends with Cr-Nb (Ref  67 ) and Ta-Ti-Cr (Ref  60 ) systems oxidized at 1200 °C, they also demonstrate unique compositional effects specific to the 1000 °C thermal regime.

Across all tested alloys, the layered oxide scale transitioned into a distinct IRZ that penetrated the substrate to varying depths (Fig.  2 ). This zone is characterized by internal reaction products, specifically nitrides in all alloys ( A1 - A5 ) and Laves phases specifically in  A2  and  A5 . The extent of these penetration depths is corroborated by EDS line scans (Fig.  6 ), which track the inward migration of oxygen and nitrogen across the sub-surface region. Representative high-magnification micrograph coupled with localized chemical analyses detailing these internal features are provided for alloy  A2  in Fig.  7 . Fig. 7 High-magnification BSE-SEM micrograph and EDS point analyses of the internal reaction products in Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2  alloy ( A2 ) after 20 h oxidation at 1000 °C

In alloy  A2 , high-magnification micrographs and EDS point analyses (Fig.  7 ) reveal the heterogeneous nature of the IRZ. Extensive needle-shaped TiN particles precipitate was clearly observed residing beneath the primary oxide scale. Specifically, Spot 1 recorded a composition of Nb 10.3, Ti 31.2, Cr 1.6, O 5.1 and N 51.8 at.%. This stoichiometry is consistent with TiN or complex Ti-Nb nitrides, evidencing nitrogen incorporation into the substrate (Ref  59 ). Conversely, Spot 2 recorded Nb 34.2, Ti 26.5, Cr 26.3 and O 12.9 at.%, an elemental ratio distinctly indicative of Laves-type intermetallic phases (Ref  78 ). The coexistence of nitrides and intermetallics within the IRZ strictly mirrors the degradation mechanisms documented by Welch et al. (Ref  60 ) and Butler et al. (Ref  67 ). These authors similarly identified internal reaction products, including acicular TiN and complex Cr 3 Nb 3 N or Cr 3 Ta 3 N, preferentially forming along phase boundaries within refractory alloys.

A direct comparison between alloys  A3  and  A2  further elucidates the competing roles of Al and Cr. Strikingly, despite a substantial 12.5 at.% Al addition, alloy  A3  developed a substantially deeper IRZ than the equivalent Cr-rich  A2 . This observation aligns with the mechanistic insights reported by Liu et al. (Ref  80 ), who demonstrated that Al-rich oxide scales in refractory alloy systems often exhibit loose, columnar morphologies and extensive cracking. These structural defects provide short-circuit diffusion pathways for both oxygen and nitrogen ingress, leading to significantly thicker internal reaction zones in Al-containing alloys when compared to Cr-doped counterparts under identical oxidation conditions.

Notably, sample  A5  exhibited the most restricted IRZ penetration (49.9 µm), suggesting that higher concentrations of scale-forming elements successfully promote the development of a denser and more continuous external barrier, thereby improving overall oxidation resistance. This ‘gettering effect’ drastically diminishes the chemical activity of oxygen and nitrogen at the sub-scale interface, favoring the formation of stable complex oxides over deleterious simple oxides. The suppressed IRZ in  A5  highlights the synergistic effect of combined Cr and Al additions in controlling the transition from an interface-limited reaction to a diffusion-controlled degradation regime. This kinetic shift is consistent with trends previously reported by Welch et al. (Ref  60 ) and Schellert et al. (Ref  22 ,  35 ).

Despite the significant reduction in mass gain, dropping from 249.52 mg cm −2  in  A1  to just 14.40 mg cm −2  in  A5 , all evaluated alloys continued to exhibit pronounced oxide spallation, indicating limited scale adherence. A potential explanation for the poor oxidation performance is the adherence of the oxide scale to the metal substrate. Butler et al. (Ref  67 ) showed that different oxide phases formed during oxidation may generate distinct PBR values, thereby inducing excessive compressive stress that inevitably discharges via sudden cracking or porosity generation. Furthermore, the presence of low-molar-volume nitrides within the IRZ (characterized by PBR < 1), could lead to porosity, cracking, and oxygen ingress. A similar effect may occur in the developed RMPEAs: continuous scale thickening, coupled with the coexistence of multiple complex oxides and internal nitrides, generates local PBR mismatches that ultimately mandate scale cracking and spallation.

Additionally, compositional differences between dendritic and interdendritic regions observed in the developed RMPEAs (Ref  54 ) may promote heterogeneous oxidation, further aggravating local stress development in the oxide scale (Ref  20 ). Due to the more negative standard Gibbs free energies (Δ G ) of oxide formation for Al, Ti, and Cr (Ref  21 ,  61 ), the interdendritic regions enriched in these elements exhibit a greater thermodynamic tendency to react with oxygen compared to the Nb-rich dendritic regions. This heterogeneous oxidation causes volume defects within the oxide scale, preventing it from acting as an effective diffusion barrier (Ref  10 ,  19 ,  20 ,  61 ). Furthermore, Lo et al. (Ref  25 ) reported that chemical heterogeneity also influences nitridation of AlCrMoNbTiSi alloy, where nitrogen preferentially diffused through Ti-rich dendritic regions, promoting the precipitation of TiN particles, whereas interdendritic regions remained less affected. This selective ingress ultimately contributed to the formation of a non-uniform IRZ, similar to that depicted in Fig.  5 .

It is worth noting that the dendritic grain refinement promoted by Cr additions (Ref  54 ) may play an important role in enhancing the oxidation resistance of the developed RMPEAs. Lu et al. (Ref  21 ) reported that small additions of yttrium (Y) to an AlMo 0.5 NbTa 0.5 TiZr alloy refined the dendritic microstructure, thereby shortening the migration distances for active elements, such as Ti and Al, from interdendritic regions toward dendritic regions. The refined dendritic crystals enabled the rapid diffusion, facilitating the formation of a dense and continuous complex oxide layer over the dendritic regions. In the present study, the refined dendritic morphology observed in the Cr-containing alloys likely contributes to the improved oxidation resistance, which is consistent with the reduced IRZ depths recorded in Fig.  2 .

sections.heading: Mechanical Behavior at 1000 °C
paragraphs: Figure  8 (a) presents the compressive stress-strain curves obtained at 1000 °C for the five developed RMPEAs, providing a comprehensive overview of their high-temperature deformation behavior. Consistent with the mechanical responses previously reported at room temperature (Ref  54 ), all evaluated alloys retained pronounced ductility at 1000 °C, successfully reaching 25% true strain without fracture. Fig. 8 Results of compression tests: (a) Stress-strain curves at 1000 °C for the developed RMPEAs; (b) Yield strength (YS) at 25 °C (Ref  54 ) and 1000 °C; (c) Main effects of Cr and Al on YS; (d) Standardized effects (ANOVA) indicating statistical factor significance and linear predictive models

As illustrated in Fig.  8 (a), the binary NbTi ( A1 ) and ternary Nb 7 Ti 7 Cr 2  ( A2 ) alloys exhibited a brief steady-state regime immediately after yielding, followed by weak strain hardening. The singular addition of 12.5 at.% Al in  A3  reduced the initial yield stress and induced a more extended stress plateau up to approximately 5% strain, similarly followed by limited strain hardening. Conversely, the quaternary alloys  A4  and  A5  exhibited more pronounced strain-hardening behavior. This response is consistent with their higher chemical complexity and increased density of obstacles to dislocation motion, such as lattice distortion and solute interactions (Ref  52 ,  81 ). Consequently, all compositions exhibited measurable strain hardening and reached maximum stress at the end of deformation.

As previously observed at room temperature by Borges et al. (Ref  54 ), the addition of Cr and Al to the binary NbTi matrix enhances mechanical strength via solid-solution strengthening mechanisms (Ref  82 ). Consequently, progressively increasing the concentration of these alloying elements proportionally elevates the yield strength, an effect directly governed by the intensification of lattice distortion and the corresponding increased resistance to dislocation mobility (Ref  83 ,  84 ,  85 - 86 ).

Figure  8 (b) compares the yield strength (YS) values extracted from the stress-strain curves at 25 and 1000 °C for the five developed RMPEAs. A pronounced reduction in YS is observed at the elevated temperature. This thermal softening is characteristic of refractory alloys subjected to thermally activated deformation. With sufficient thermal energy, dislocations overcome short-range barriers, resulting in reduced resistance to plastic deformation (Ref  87 ).

Although the solid-solution strengthening effect imparted by Cr is attenuated at 1000 °C (Ref  26 ,  81 ), its contribution remains significant. Alloys  A2  and  A5 , both containing 12.5 at.% Cr, exhibited the highest YS values at 1000 °C (254.5 and 229.0 MPa, respectively). Alloy  A2  demonstrated a marginal strength advantage, likely attributable to the absence of Al. In contrast, alloys  A1 ,  A3 , and  A4 , which contain lower or no Cr, underwent more pronounced thermal softening. Notably, alloy  A3  (12.5 at.% Al) exhibited the poorest performance, indicating that Al additions preferentially facilitate thermally activated softening mechanisms.

Figure  8 (c) shows the main effect plots of Cr and Al on the YS at both room temperature and 1000 °C, obtained from the DOE 2 2  factorial design with a central point (Ref  88 ,  89 ). Across both thermal regimes, increasing the Cr concentration from 0 to 12.5 at.% results in a substantial increase in YS, confirming Cr as the primary strengthening element within this multicomponent system. Conversely, the strengthening contribution of Al exhibits strong temperature dependence. At room temperature, Al positively contributes to the YS, albeit with a lower potency than Cr. However, at 1000 °C, Al exerts a slightly negative effect, leading to reduced mechanical strength. This mechanistic reversal indicates that, at elevated temperature, Al ceases to function as a viable strengthening agent and instead promotes thermal softening.

As discussed by Fitzner et al. (Ref  90 ), Al concentrations exceeding 10 at.% effectively suppress twinning in Ti-based alloys, completely eliminating a critical strain-hardening mechanism. Consequently, at 1000 °C, deformation is expected to proceed predominantly via dislocation slip, a mechanism that is readily activated under high-thermal-energy conditions. Furthermore, the central points within the factorial design remained strictly aligned with the established linear trends, indicating negligible curvature and validating an essentially linear response surface within the specific compositional space investigated.

Figure  8 (d) illustrates the standardized effects of Cr, Al, and their interaction (Cr*Al), mapping these against a 95% significance threshold ( α  = 0.05) indicated by a red line. Effects exceeding this threshold are considered statistically significant (Ref  88 ,  89 ). The corresponding ANOVA analysis reveals that the mechanical performance of the Nb-Ti-(Cr)-(Al) RMPEAs is predominantly controlled by the isolated main effect of Cr at both testing temperatures, whereas the isolated effect of Al remains strictly temperature-dependent. Crucially, the absence of a statistically significant Cr*Al interaction term indicates that Cr and Al operate independently and additively within the studied compositional range. Consequently, the final YS predictive models at 1000 °C were successfully fitted using a multilinear approximation ( R 2  > 0.98), yielding specific strengthening coefficients that quantitatively assess the mechanical effectiveness of each respective element.

Specifically, the addition of Cr into the binary NbTi system resulted in a strengthening coefficient of 34.518 MPa/at.% at room temperature; however, this value decreased by nearly half to 15.397 MPa/at.% at 1000 °C. By contrast, while the addition of Al to NbTi generated a positive strengthening coefficient of 11.982 MPa/at.% at room temperature, this coefficient inverted to a negative value (− 1.411 MPa/at.%) at 1000 °C, confirming the mechanism change at elevated temperature.

sections.heading: Comparison of Mass Gain and Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: A comparison of mass gain between the developed RMPEAs and several advanced RHEAs/RMPEAs is presented in Fig.  9 . Relative to the oxidation behavior of CrMoNbTaTiZr alloy at 1000 °C reported by Senkov et al. (Ref  17 ), CrMo 0.5 NbTa 0.5 TiZr suffered from extremely high mass gain due to the absence of a protective oxide layer, the binary NbTi ( A1 ) alloy exhibited a similarly poor response. Fig. 9 Comparison of mass gain among various RMPEAs oxidized at 1000 °C for 20 h, benchmarking literature data (Ref  16 ,  17 - 18 ,  59 ,  61 ,  72 ,  91 ,  92 ,  93 - 94 ) against the RMPEAs developed in the present work

In contrast, a comparison of oxide architectures reveals that the alloys incorporating Cr and Al ( A2 - A5 ) demonstrated a tendency toward selective oxidation, forming complex oxides that yielded superior oxidation resistance. Specifically, Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  ( A5 ) benefited from a combined 25.0 at.% addition of Cr and Al, which effectively resisted oxidation and nitridation within the BCC matrix, thereby minimizing the extent of the IRZ. Consequently, the mass gain of  A5  during 1000 °C exposure was significantly reduced.

When compared with more recently developed oxidation-resistant RMPEAs containing similar constituents, the performance of alloy  A5  after 20 h at 1000 °C surpassed that of AlNbTiCrZr and positioned itself intermediate to AlCrMoTiW and AlCrMoNbTi. These previous works suggested that parabolic mass gain rates observed for the oxidation of MPEAs could be attributed to the formation of protective Al 2 O 3  and Cr 2 O 3  on the alloy surface, although no detailed microstructural characterizations were reported (Ref  71 ,  94 ). Nevertheless, the oxidation resistance of  A5  remains inferior to that of alloys within the Al-Cr-Mo-Ta-Ti system, wherein the formation of a dense and protective CrTaO 4 -based oxide layer provides enhanced scale stability (Ref  22 ,  25 ,  30 ,  59 ,  61 ).

Figure  10  shows the materials property space of several RMPEAs as a function of density, comparing the yield strength at room-temperature and 1000 °C in Fig.  10 (a), and the room-temperature compressive plastic strain in Fig.  10 (b). The inclusion of Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  alloy ( A5 ) highlights a remarkable combination of low density (< 7 g cm −3 ), high room-temperature ductility (> 30% strain) (Ref  30 ), and competitive yield strength at 1000 °C relative to other lightweight Ti- and Nb-based systems (Ref  29 ,  95 ). Among RMPEAs, those that exhibit higher high-temperature strength commonly show limited room-temperature ductility. In contrast, the RMPEAs developed herein achieve a distinguishable balance of low density, room-temperature ductility and pronounced high-temperature strength, an uncommon characteristic in refractory BCC MPEAs (Ref  29 ,  95 ). Additionally, the high-temperature mechanical performance of alloy  A5  surpasses that of benchmark commercial Ni-based superalloys at 1000 °C, projecting its capabilities beyond the operational limits of conventional superalloy systems. Fig. 10 Materials property space for RMPEAs as a function of density: (a) Yield strength (YS, MPa) at room temperature and 1000 °C; (b) Room-temperature compressive plastic strain ( ε , %). Literature data for RMPEAs and Ni-based alloys (Ref  26 ,  95 ) are compared with the Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  alloy ( A5 ) developed in the present work

For context, Senkov et al. (Ref  46 ) investigated a series of lightweight RHEAs within the Cr-Nb-Ti-V-Zr system, exhibiting densities ranging from 6.34 and 6.67 g cm −3 . In their study, the Cr-free NbTiVZr and NbTiV 2 Zr alloys showed yield strengths of 58 and 72 MPa at 1000 °C, respectively, whereas the Cr-containing CrNbTiZr and CrNbTiVZr alloys achieved considerably higher strengths of 115 and 259 MPa. Nevertheless, while those Cr-free compositions retained high room-temperature ductility (> 50% strain), the corresponding Cr-bearing variants fractured at strains below 10%. This reduction in ductility was attributed to the tendency of Cr to promote the formation of brittle Laves phases (Ref  46 ). By contrast, the Cr-containing RMPEAs developed in the present study successfully demonstrate enhanced high-temperature strength without inducing any apparent loss of ductility.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The oxidation and compressive mechanical behavior of five low-density (~ 6.5 g cm −3 ) Nb-Ti-(Cr)-(Al) RMPEAs, which possess intrinsic room-temperature ductility, were systematically investigated at 1000 °C. Based on the experimental results and microstructural characterization, the following principal conclusions are drawn: The binary NbTi reference alloy ( A1 ) forms a permeable, non-protective oxide scale dominated by TiO 2  and TiNb 2 O 7 . The defective scale facilitates extensive ingress of oxygen and nitrogen, culminating in the development of a deep internal IRZ that compromises the entire substrate. The individual and combined additions of Cr and Al significantly enhance oxidation resistance relative to the binary NbTi base alloy. Notably, the Nb 3 Ti 3 Cr 1 Al 1  alloy ( A5 ) demonstrated the superior oxidation performance, achieving the lowest mass gain, the smallest IRZ depth, and reduced kinetic exponents. Nevertheless, oxide-scale spallation persists in all compositions, indicating that scale adherence remains a critical limitation. Chromium exerts a dominant role in enhancing oxidation resistance by promoting the stabilization of Cr-rich oxides, which function as effective diffusion barriers. Conversely, a singular addition of 12.5 at.% Al is insufficient to form a continuous and stable Al 2 O 3  scale; however, when combined with Cr, Al further improves the oxidation resistance through the formation of more complex mixed oxide scales. All investigated RMPEAs maintain ductility during compression at 1000 °C. The Cr-containing compositions exhibited superior yield strength, demonstrating that Cr-induced solid-solution strengthening mechanisms remain effective even under thermally activated deformation. Ultimately, the Nb-Ti-(Cr)-(Al) RMPEAs investigated in this study achieve a rare and highly desirable balance of properties for structural application: a relatively low density (substantially lighter than conventional Ni-based superalloys), with intrinsic room-temperature ductility, and competitive mechanical strength at 1000 °C. However, further improvements are still required to enhance oxidation resistance.
